source_text:
ἐάν τε γὰρ ἀπολογοῦμαι ἐγκαλούμενος διὰ τοὺς πιστεύοντας ων καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐστε, ἐάν
τε βεβαιοῦν βούλομαι τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν τισιν, ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας ἐνστάσεως· ἐάν τε
δεικνύναι οτι οὐκ ἀνονήτως ὑπομένω δεσμούς, ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας πίστεως. Phil 2,7
Καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ανθρωπος. τὸ ὡς οὐχ ὁμοιώσεώς ἐστιν ἀλλ' ἐπιτάσεως, οιόν
ἐστι τὸ ὡς ἀγαθὸς ὁ θεὸς τῷ ̓Ισραήλ, καὶ ὡς ἠγάπησα τὸν νόμον σου, κύριε, ἀντὶ τοῦ
πάνυ ἠγάπησα. Phil 2,16 ̓Αντὶ τοῦ προσέχοντες τῷ λόγῳ τῆς ζωῆς. καὶ τῷ Τιμοθέῳ δὲ
γράφει· επεχε σεαυτῷ, ἀντὶ τοῦ πρόσεχε σεαυτῷ. Phil 3,8a Εἰ διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ζημίαν
ἡγεῖται, οὐκ ην κακά· ην γὰρ κέρδη. καὶ ηγημαι ειπεν· οὐ γὰρ ην ζημία, ἀλλὰ κατὰ
παράθεσιν τῆς ὑπερβολῆς τῶν κρειττόνων ἡγεῖται ζημίαν. 314 Phil 3,8b Τὸ
σκύβαλον μέρος ἐστι καλάμης, ἡ δὲ καλάμη καὶ ὁ στάχυς ποτὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ σπόρου.
thought_title: Paul's proofs from the Philippians' faith and steadfastness
orientation: Severianus is explaining how Paul uses the Philippians' faith and steadfastness to show that his sufferings and defense of the gospel are not fruitless.
pass_a_gloss: For whether I make my defense when accused because of those who believe, of whom you also are, or whether I wish to confirm the gospel to some, from your steadfastness; or whether to show that I do not endure bonds without profit, from your faith. Phil 2,7 And being found in form truly a human. The 'truly' is not of likeness but of intensity, such as is 'truly good is God to Israel,' and 'truly I loved your law, Lord,' instead of 'I loved very much.' Phil 2,16 Instead of 'attending to the word of life.' And to Timothy he writes: 'pay attention to yourself,' instead of 'attend to yourself.' Phil 3,8a If because of Christ he considers it loss, they were not bad; for they were gains. And he said 'I have considered'; for it was not loss, but by comparison with the excess of the better things he considers it loss. 314 Phil 3,8b The rubbish is a part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear of grain once from the seed.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'truly' for ὡς in Philippians 2:7, where Severianus argues it expresses intensity, not likeness.
The glossary requires 'steadfastness' for ἔνστασις, the Philippians' firm stand in faith.
The glossary requires 'rubbish' for σκύβαλον, used here as part of the agricultural image of chaff-like elements.
The glossary requires 'stalk' for καλάμη, representing the prophets in the agricultural image.
The glossary requires 'ear of grain' for στάχυς, representing Christ in the image.
The glossary requires 'seed' for σπόρος, the seed of Abraham's faith.

pass_b_english: For whether I make my defense when I am accused for the sake of those who believe—and you are among them—or whether I want to confirm the gospel to some, I do so from your steadfastness. Or whether I want to show that I do not endure chains without profit, I do so from your faith. (Philippians 1:7)

“And being found in form as a human” (Philippians 2:7). The word “as” does not express likeness but intensity; it means “truly.” It is like the phrase “truly good is God to Israel,” and “truly I have loved your law, Lord,” meaning “I have loved it very much.”

“Holding fast the word of life” (Philippians 2:16) means “paying attention to the word of life.” And to Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16), meaning “attend to yourself.”

If he counts it as loss for the sake of Christ, it was not evil; for it was gains. And he said “I have counted.” For it was not loss, but in comparison with the surpassing greatness of better things he counts it as loss.
Rubbish is a part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear of grain once came from the seed.

problems.quote: And being found in form truly human
problems.why: Source says 'found in form as a human'; English merges 'form' with 'truly' and drops 'as', misrepresenting the quoted verse.
problems.fix: And being found in form as a human
problems.ruling: Source quotes ὡς ἄνθρωπος 'as a human'; English 'truly human' changes grammar and drops 'as', misquoting.

problems.quote: The word “truly” does not express likeness but intensity.
problems.source_quote: τὸ ὡς οὐχ ὁμοιώσεώς ἐστιν ἀλλ' ἐπιτάσεως
problems.why: Glossary requires 'truly' for ὡς; the English should say the word 'as' (ὡς) is rendered 'truly', not that 'truly' itself is the word discussed.
problems.fix: The word 'as' does not express likeness but intensity; it means 'truly.'
problems.ruling: Source discusses ὡς 'as'; English 'truly' misidentifies the lemma, breaking glossary reference to ὡς.

problems.source_quote: καὶ ἡγημαι εἶπεν· οὐ γὰρ ἦν ζημία, ἀλλὰ κατὰ παράθεσιν τῆς ὑπερβολῆς τῶν κρειττόνων ἡγεῖται ζημίαν
problems.why: The English merges καὶ ἡγημαι εἶπεν with the following clause, but 'And he said "I have counted"' is present. Actually looking again: English has 'And he said "I have counted." For it was not loss...' This renders καὶ ἡγημαι εἶπεν as 'And he said "I have counted."' But ἡγημαι is 'I have counted', so the quote should be 'I have counted' not 'he said I have counted'. Actually the Greek says καὶ ἡγημαι εἶπεν which is odd - 'and "I have counted" he said' or 'and he said "I have counted"'. The English is fine.

edits.old: And being found in form truly human
edits.new: And being found in form as a human

edits.old: The word “truly” does not express likeness but intensity.
edits.new: The word “as” does not express likeness but intensity; it means “truly.”

fixed: The reported omission about 'And he said "I have counted"' is not a real problem; the English already renders the Greek correctly.

problems.quote: paying attention to the word of life
problems.why: Same Greek root (προσέχω) rendered two ways; reader may miss parallel.
problems.fix: Use 'attend to' for both or note equivalence.

variants.text: paying attention to the word of life

problems.quote: I make proof of your steadfastness
problems.why: Same construction varies: 'make proof of,' 'from,' mixing 'faith' and 'steadfastness' as sources.
problems.fix: Standardize preposition and clarify whether faith/steadfastness are synonyms here.

variants.text: I make proof of your steadfastness
I do so from your steadfastness
I do so from your faith

problems.quote: Rubbish is a part of the stalk
problems.why: Skubala normally means dung/excrement, not stalk; agricultural reading is Severianus's creative interpretation, not standard meaning.
problems.fix: Add note that this is allegorical redefinition of 'rubbish/skubala'.

problems.quote: From your faith I make proof of your steadfastness.
problems.why: Reader cannot tell if this is Paul's words, Severianus's summary, or a paraphrase of Phil 1:7.
problems.fix: Mark as Severianus's paraphrase of Paul's point in Phil 1:7.

problems.quote: For whether I make my defense when I am accused for the sake of those who believe—and you are among them—or whether I want to confirm the gospel to some, I do so from your steadfastness.
problems.why: Presented as if quoting Paul but does not match Phil 1:7's wording; unclear if paraphrase or Severianus's expansion.
problems.fix: Mark as Severianus's interpretive paraphrase of Phil 1:7.

problems.quote: If he counts it as loss for the sake of Christ, it was not evil; for it was gains.
problems.why: Logic is circular and pronouns unclear; 'it was gains' seems to contradict 'counts it as loss.'
problems.fix: Clarify: Paul's former gains were not evil but are counted loss compared to Christ.

problems.quote: Rubbish is a part of the stalk
problems.why: 'Rubbish' for chaff/husk misleads; modern reader thinks garbage, not grain residue.
problems.fix: Use 'chaff' or 'husk' instead of 'rubbish' for the agricultural sense.

problems.quote: And to Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16)
problems.why: 1 Tim 4:16 reads 'Pay close attention to yourself and to the teaching'; 'Pay attention to yourself' is partial.
problems.fix: Note it is a partial quotation of 1 Timothy 4:16.

edits.old: For whether I make my defense when I am accused for the sake of those who believe—and you are among them—or whether I want to confirm the gospel to some, I do so from your steadfastness. Or whether I want to show that I do not endure chains without profit, I do so from your faith. (Philippians 1:7)
edits.new: Severianus paraphrases Paul's point in Philippians 1:7: whether I make my defense when I am accused for the sake of those who believe—and you are among them—or whether I want to confirm the gospel to some, I do so from your steadfastness. Or whether I want to show that I do not endure chains without profit, I do so from your faith.

edits.old: “Holding fast the word of life” (Philippians 2:16) means “paying attention to the word of life.” And to Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16), meaning “attend to yourself.”
edits.new: “Holding fast the word of life” (Philippians 2:16) means “attending to the word of life.” And to Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16), meaning “attend to yourself.”

edits.old: If he counts it as loss for the sake of Christ, it was not evil; for it was gains. And he said “I have counted.” For it was not loss, but in comparison with the surpassing greatness of better things he counts it as loss.
edits.new: If he counts it as loss for the sake of Christ, his former gains were not evil; for they were gains. And he said “I have counted.” For it was not loss, but in comparison with the surpassing greatness of better things he counts it as loss.

edits.old: Rubbish is a part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear of grain once came from the seed.
edits.new: Severianus here redefines “rubbish” allegorically: rubbish is a part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear of grain once came from the seed.

edits.old: And to Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16), meaning “attend to yourself.”
edits.new: And to Timothy he also writes, “Pay attention to yourself” (1 Timothy 4:16, a partial quotation), meaning “attend to yourself.”

fixed: The glossary problem about 'paying attention' vs 'attend' was real; I standardized the English to 'attending' in the main text and adjusted the gloss to match.
The problem about mixing 'make proof of' and 'from' was not present in the current English; the text already uses 'from' consistently for both faith and steadfastness.
The speaker problem about the opening paraphrase was real; I marked it as Severianus's paraphrase of Philippians 1:7.
The unreadable logic problem was real; I clarified that 'it' refers to Paul's former gains.

The mistranslation problem about 'rubbish' as chaff was not a mistranslation of the source, since the source itself uses σκύβαλον and the glossary mandates 'rubbish'; I added a note that this is Severianus's allegorical redefinition.
The wrong_scripture problem about 1 Timothy 4:16 was real; I noted it is a partial quotation.

last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ τῷ Τιμοθέῳ δὲ γράφει· ἔπεχε σεαυτῷ
last_rejected.why: Source says 'Pay attention to yourself' is written to Timothy, but 1 Tim 4:16 reads differently; no formal citation given.
last_rejected.fix: Remove the reference or cite correctly per source intent.
last_rejected.ruling: Source has no formal citation; translator supplied plausible reference for Timothy quote, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: Holding fast the word of life
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἀντὶ τοῦ προσέχοντες τῷ λόγῳ τῆς ζωῆς
last_rejected.why: Source says 'paying attention to' (προσέχοντες), not 'holding fast'. English inverts meaning.
last_rejected.fix: 'Paying attention to the word of life' means 'giving heed to the word of life.'
last_rejected.ruling: Source quotes Phil 2:16 as 'Holding fast'; translator renders the biblical text accurately, then glosses προσέχοντες as 'paying attention.'

last_rejected.quote: For whether I make my defense
last_rejected.why: English hides that these are Paul's words being quoted. No quotation marks or attribution to Paul.
last_rejected.ruling: Source ἐάν τε γὰρ ἀπολογοῦμαι is indirect discourse; no explicit quotation marks in Greek. Omission is stylistic, not meaning-changing.

last_rejected.quote: If he counts it as loss
last_rejected.source_quote: Εἰ διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ζημίαν ἡγεῖται, οὐκ ἦν κακά
last_rejected.why: English omits 'for the sake of Christ' (διὰ τὸν Χριστόν), crucial to Paul's argument.
last_rejected.fix: If for the sake of Christ he counts it as loss, it was not evil
last_rejected.ruling: English 'counts it as loss for the sake of Christ' includes διὰ τὸν Χριστόν. The claim is factually wrong; nothing is omitted.

last_rejected.why: English omits 'for' (γάρ), weakening the causal connection.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'For it was not loss' renders γάρ as 'For.' The claim is factually wrong; nothing is omitted.

last_rejected.quote: in comparison with the surpassing greatness of better things
last_rejected.source_quote: κατὰ παράθεσιν τῆς ὑπερβολῆς τῶν κρειττόνων
last_rejected.why: 'surpassing greatness' overtranslates ὑπερβολή; 'excess' or 'surpassing quality' better. But 'surpassing greatness' is within semantic range.
last_rejected.fix: in comparison with the surpassing quality of better things
last_rejected.ruling: 'Surpassing greatness' is within normal range of ὑπερβολή. Mere preference, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: Rubbish is a part of the stalk
last_rejected.why: Biologically wrong: chaff/rubbish is not part of stalk. But this is what source says, so English correct. However 'part of' could mean 'belongs to the same plant as'.
last_rejected.fix: Rubbish is a part of the stalk
last_rejected.ruling: Source says σκύβαλον μέρος ἐστι καλάμης; English 'part of the stalk' is faithful. Biological accuracy irrelevant to translation.
